about: Answer-quality scenarios grown from real ratings. Each one states a question and the properties any acceptable answer must and must not have. Properties are semantic: a grader model judges them on meaning, never on wording, so an answer that satisfies a property in its own words passes. Run with scripts/evaluate-answer-quality.mjs. Candidates mined from downvotes land in candidates.json and are promoted into this file by hand — see README.md for why that step is not automated.

reasons.wrong: The answer asserted something the material did not support.
reasons.too_long: The answer was correct but buried.
reasons.missed_point: The answer addressed a different question than the one asked.
reasons.style: The register or shape was wrong. Properties for these are written by a reviewer; there is no subject-independent rule for register.

scenarios.note: The answer-depth contract ends with an explicit restraint: a one-fact question still gets the fact. This scenario exists to catch the overcorrection where a gate meant to add depth turns every short question into a survey.
scenarios.question: How many bytes long is an IPv6 address?

must: States that an IPv6 address is 16 bytes (128 bits).
Gives that figure in the first sentence.
mustNot: Opens with background on IPv6, its history, or why the question is being asked.
Surveys IPv4, address notation, or subnetting before answering.
Runs past a short paragraph.

scenarios.note: A constraint stated in the question is part of the question. Answering the more familiar version of an ask is the most common way a technically correct answer misses the point.
scenarios.question: Name three programming languages in common use that have no garbage collector. Do not mention Rust.

must: Names exactly three languages that are in common use and are not garbage collected.
Honours the exclusion: Rust is not among the three named.
mustNot: Names Rust, including as an aside, a recommendation, or a fourth example.
Substitutes a different question, such as which languages are memory safe or which are fastest.
Asks why Rust is excluded before answering.

scenarios.note: The failure this catches is not inventing a fact but answering a question the supplied material is silent on, in the confident register the rest of the material invites.
scenarios.question: Here is the tail of a failed deploy log. Did this build run out of memory?
scenarios.evidence:
2026-04-11T09:14:02Z  info   resolving dependencies (412 packages)
2026-04-11T09:14:58Z  info   compiling 1,204 modules
2026-04-11T09:17:31Z  warn   chunk "vendor" is 4.2 MB after minification
2026-04-11T09:19:04Z  info   emitting build artifacts
2026-04-11T09:19:40Z  error  worker exited unexpectedly (signal SIGKILL)
2026-04-11T09:19:40Z  error  build failed after 5m38s

must: States that the log does not record memory usage and therefore does not settle the question.
Identifies SIGKILL as consistent with an out-of-memory kill without asserting that is what happened.
Names at least one concrete thing that would settle it, such as the host's kernel log or the container's exit reason.
mustNot: States as fact that the build ran out of memory.
States as fact that the build did not run out of memory.
Treats the large vendor chunk as evidence of the cause.

scenarios.note: Cross-subject teaching regression: assess the actual reasoning, prerequisite order and requested scope. This is synthetic evaluation material, not a private conversation export.
scenarios.question: Teach me Bayes theorem. I understand fractions and percentages but conditional probability confuses me. Use a spam filter as the example.

must: Uses hypothetical counts to establish the reference group for each conditional probability.
Derives the probability of spam among flagged messages by counting both spam and non-spam ways to receive a flag.
Connects that calculation to the general formula without requiring unexplained notation.
mustNot: Confuses the proportion of spam caught with the proportion of flagged messages that are spam.
Presents illustrative filter rates as measured facts.

scenarios.question: Why does a plant cell swell when put in pure water? I know cells have a membrane and a wall, but I have not studied osmosis.

must: Explains selective permeability and distinguishes movement both ways from net inward movement.
Connects dissolved solutes to the direction of net movement through an intelligible physical principle or mechanism, rather than restating that water tends to enter.
Explains how rising internal pressure and the cell wall limit swelling.
mustNot: Attributes intentions to water molecules.
Claims that no molecules cross at equilibrium or that the cell wall is the selectively permeable barrier.

scenarios.question: I know Python loops and functions. Teach me recursion using a folder that can contain files and more folders.

must: Motivates recursion through the repeated task of counting files inside nested folders.
Traces a concrete nested call and return, explaining the caller resuming with its own state.
Explains both the stopping case and progress toward it, including empty folders under the stated tree assumptions.
mustNot: Only gives code and defines recursion as a function calling itself.
Claims that every possible filesystem is a finite acyclic folder tree.

scenarios.question: What is the difference between "I lived here for five years" and "I have lived here for five years"? English is my second language. Keep it to a few paragraphs.

must: Uses situations to explain how the two time intervals relate to the present.
Distinguishes the usual implication of no longer living there from a logical guarantee.
Keeps the answer to a few paragraphs at a suitable level for an English learner.
mustNot: Only labels the two tenses without explaining their meaning.
Forces a mathematical derivation or unrelated prerequisite lesson.

scenarios.question: Write a connected explanation of why the fictional town of Merrow changed its water system, using all the relevant evidence in this packet. I want to understand the causes, not a list of dates.
scenarios.evidence:
Record A, council minutes, 1880: The old communal wells supplied drinking water. The council rejected a pipe proposal because the initial construction cost was too high.
Record B, maintenance accounts, 1882: Two wells repeatedly failed during dry months. Repairs and carted water cost twice the annual estimate.
Record C, merchants petition, 1883: Shopkeepers asked for more reliable water for daily work. The petition did not mention illness.
Record D, council minutes, 1884: A grant paid half the upfront cost of pipes. The council approved a piped supply, citing reliability and the reduced local construction bill.
Appendix, household letters, 1885: Some poorer households still used a working communal well because they could not afford the connection fee.
Unrelated appendix: The town painted its clock tower blue in 1884.

must: Connects unreliable wells, changed costs, the petition and the grant to the council decision.
Includes the later household evidence and explains why building the system did not guarantee everyone could connect.
Keeps documented reasons distinct from plausible inference.
mustNot: Invents an illness outbreak or a health campaign.
Uses the unrelated clock-tower color as a cause of the water-system change.

scenarios.question: Write a first-principles lesson on sinusoidal steady-state AC circuit analysis, including impedance and reactance. I know DC resistors, current, voltage and basic derivatives, but I have not used complex numbers in circuits. Use one circuit to connect the ideas.

must: Establishes a concrete AC circuit problem that a single real resistance cannot fully describe.
Makes amplitude and phase meaningful and motivates complex notation before relying on it.
Derives an element voltage-current relation for a sinusoid and uses it to construct impedance.
Explains reactance through out-of-phase voltage/current and reversible energy storage, not only its name or imaginary-part definition.
Returns to the same circuit with an interpreted prediction and states the sinusoidal steady-state assumptions.
mustNot: Introduces impedance only as a table of formulas to substitute.
Treats reactance as resistive energy dissipation.

scenarios.note: Promoted from the completed 2026-09-30 independent instruction-cleanup comparison. This synthetic case is now a development regression, not an unseen holdout. Candidate answers improved concreteness but one used undefined symbols.
scenarios.question: Explain why a solid steel nail sinks but a steel ship can float. I know about mass, volume, gravity and pressure increasing with depth. Build a connected explanation rather than just naming Archimedes' principle.

must: Builds the upward imbalance of pressure forces into buoyant force before relying on the name.
Connects displaced water volume and equilibrium to the ship's shape and total weight, then contrasts the solid nail.
Distinguishes the submerged external volume of a hollow hull from the volume of steel alone.
Gives a usable meaning to every symbol needed in the central argument when introducing it.
mustNot: Claims gravity is absent, that the water supports every object, or that hollowness alone guarantees flotation.
Only names Archimedes' principle or average density without explaining the force or volume connection.

scenarios.note: Promoted from the completed 2026-09-30 independent instruction-cleanup comparison. This synthetic case is now a development regression, not an unseen holdout. One candidate introduced a power rule in its application without establishing it.
scenarios.question: I understand powers such as 2^3=8 but I have never understood logarithms. Explain what they are, why multiplying numbers turns into adding logarithms, and when that helps. Please build the ideas from what I know.

must: Defines a logarithm as the exponent needed for a fixed positive base other than one, with positive real arguments in this setting.
Derives the product rule from exponent addition through a concrete example and connects it to the general relationship.
Gives an application in which converting multiplication to addition has an explained purpose.
Establishes any additional logarithm rule essential to its chosen application before relying on it.
mustNot: Treats the product rule as the definition of logarithms or claims logs distribute over addition.
Uses an unexplained rule to solve the application after promising to build from powers.

scenarios.note: Promoted from the completed 2026-09-30 independent instruction-cleanup comparison. This synthetic case is now a development regression, not an unseen holdout. All four baseline/candidate generations asserted that organized lookup is fast without showing the narrowing decisions.
scenarios.question: I have a table containing a million customer records. Why can adding an index make looking up one customer faster, yet make adding customers slower? I know what a table and a sorted list are, but not database internals.

must: Shows the work required by a scan and by a concrete indexed lookup, including how a comparison or branch decision rules out records without reading each one.
Explains the additional stored lookup structure and how its entries lead to the actual customer row.
Connects slower writes to maintaining that structure, with a concrete insertion or update example.
Makes clear that an index helps suitable lookups and need not improve every query.
mustNot: Only asserts that sorted or tree search is faster without demonstrating the search mechanism.
Claims that every database index is a hash table or that every query is accelerated.

scenarios.note: Teaching applies to requests for understanding, not every sentence containing a technical term.
scenarios.question: Correct only the spelling in this sentence and return only the corrected sentence: An explanaton of memory and impulse responce.

must: Returns exactly: An explanation of memory and impulse response.
mustNot: Adds an explanation of either term, a preamble, or an offer.
